class C_Recipe {
  name: string;
  ingredients: string;
  steps: string;
}
</classes>
<fields>
c_selected: number = -1
</fields>
<functions>
function c_recipeList(): C_Recipe[] {
  let out: C_Recipe[] = [];
  out.push({name: "Garlic Butter Pasta", ingredients: "pasta|garlic|butter|parmesan|salt", steps: "Boil the pasta in salted water. Melt butter with sliced garlic. Toss the drained pasta in the garlic butter and finish with grated parmesan."});
  out.push({name: "Tomato Egg Scramble", ingredients: "eggs|tomato|onion|oil|salt", steps: "Beat the eggs. Soften onion in oil, add chopped tomato and cook down. Pour in the eggs and stir gently until just set."});
  out.push({name: "Chickpea Salad", ingredients: "chickpeas|tomato|cucumber|lemon|olive oil", steps: "Drain the chickpeas. Dice tomato and cucumber. Toss everything with lemon juice, olive oil and a pinch of salt."});
  out.push({name: "Cheese Omelette", ingredients: "eggs|cheese|butter|milk|pepper", steps: "Whisk eggs with milk and pepper. Melt butter in a pan, pour in the eggs, scatter cheese and fold when nearly set."});
  out.push({name: "Rice and Beans", ingredients: "rice|beans|onion|garlic|cumin", steps: "Cook the rice. Fry onion and garlic with cumin, add the beans and a splash of water, then serve over the rice."});
  out.push({name: "Simple Pancakes", ingredients: "flour|milk|eggs|sugar|butter", steps: "Whisk flour, milk, eggs and sugar into a smooth batter. Cook ladlefuls in a buttered pan until golden on both sides."});
  return out;
}

function c_hasIngredient(state: AppState, name: string): boolean {
  let want: string = strings.toLowerCase(strings.trim(name));
  for (let e: LogEntry of state.entries) {
    if (strings.toLowerCase(strings.trim(e.ingredient)) === want) { return true; }
  }
  return false;
}

function c_ingredientCount(recipe: C_Recipe): number {
  let parts: string[] = strings.split(recipe.ingredients, "|");
  return parts.length();
}

function c_haveCount(state: AppState, recipe: C_Recipe): number {
  let parts: string[] = strings.split(recipe.ingredients, "|");
  let have: number = 0;
  for (let p: string of parts) {
    if (c_hasIngredient(state, p)) { have = have + 1; }
  }
  return have;
}

function c_missingCount(state: AppState, recipe: C_Recipe): number {
  let m: number = c_ingredientCount(recipe) - c_haveCount(state, recipe);
  if (m < 0) { return 0; }
  return m;
}

function c_canCook(state: AppState, recipe: C_Recipe): number {
  if (c_missingCount(state, recipe) <= state.maxMissing) { return 1; }
  return 0;
}

function c_missingList(state: AppState, recipe: C_Recipe): string {
  let parts: string[] = strings.split(recipe.ingredients, "|");
  let text: string = "";
  for (let p: string of parts) {
    if (!c_hasIngredient(state, p)) {
      if (text === "") {
        text = strings.trim(p);
      } else {
        text = text + ", " + strings.trim(p);
      }
    }
  }
  if (text === "") { return "Nothing missing."; }
  return "Missing: " + text;
}

function c_selectRecipe(state: AppState, value: number): AppState {
  if (state.c_selected === value) {
    return {c_selected: -1__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  return {c_selected: value__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_addMissing(state: AppState, value: number): AppState {
  let recipes: C_Recipe[] = c_recipeList();
  if (value < 0 || value >= recipes.length()) {
    return {c_selected: state.c_selected__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  let recipe: C_Recipe = recipes[value];
  let parts: string[] = strings.split(recipe.ingredients, "|");
  let out: LogEntry[] = [];
  for (let e: LogEntry of state.entries) { out.push(e); }
  let minute: number = time.hourOfDay() * 60 + time.minuteOfHour();
  for (let p: string of parts) {
    if (!c_hasIngredient(state, p)) {
      out.push({ingredient: strings.trim(p), minute: minute});
    }
  }
  return {entries: out__PASSTHROUGH__};
}
</functions>
<view>
{
  let recipes: C_Recipe[] = c_recipeList();
  if (state.entries.length() === 0) {
    sections.push(ui.Section("content", "", "", [
      ui.Text("body", "Add the ingredients you have above, and each recipe below will show how many you already have and whether you can cook it now.")
    ]));
  }
  let rows: ui.View[] = [];
  let i: number = 0;
  while (i < recipes.length()) {
    let r: C_Recipe = recipes[i];
    let need: number = c_ingredientCount(r);
    let have: number = c_haveCount(state, r);
    let missing: number = c_missingCount(state, r);
    let can: number = c_canCook(state, r);
    let trailer: string = ui.numberToString(missing) + " missing";
    if (can === 1) { trailer = "Can cook now"; }
    let sub: string = ui.numberToString(have) + " of " + ui.numberToString(need) + " ingredients on hand";
    rows.push(ui.ListItem("default", r.name, sub, trailer, "c_selectRecipe", i, true, "list"));
    if (state.c_selected === i) {
      let canWord: string = "No";
      if (can === 1) { canWord = "Yes"; }
      let detail: ui.View[] = [];
      let ingRows: ui.View[] = [];
      let parts: string[] = strings.split(r.ingredients, "|");
      for (let p: string of parts) {
        let haveIt: boolean = c_hasIngredient(state, p);
        let mark: string = "Missing";
        let tone: string = "warning";
        if (haveIt) { mark = "On hand"; tone = "success"; }
        ingRows.push(ui.ListItem(tone, strings.trim(p), "", mark, "", 0, true, ""));
      }
      detail.push(ui.SectionHeader("default", "Ingredients", "", ui.numberToString(need)));
      detail.push(ui.ListGroup("default", "", ingRows));
      detail.push(ui.KeyValueGroup("default", 2, [
        ui.KeyValueItem("default", "Still missing", ui.numberToString(missing), "ingredients you do not have"),
        ui.KeyValueItem("default", "Can cook now", canWord, "allows up to " + ui.numberToString(state.maxMissing) + " missing")
      ]));

      detail.push(ui.Text("body", r.steps));

          ui.Button("secondary", "Add missing to pantry", "c_addMissing", i, true)
        ]));
      }
      rows.push(ui.Card("surface", [ui.Column("default", detail)]));
    }
    i = i + 1;
  }
  sections.push(ui.Section("content", "", "", [
    ui.SectionHeader("default", "Recipes", "Tap one to see its full ingredient list", ui.numberToString(recipes.length())),

<classes>
@jsonable
class C_Recipe {
  name: string;
  ingredients: string;
  steps: string;
}
</classes>
<fields>
c_selected: number = -1
</fields>
<functions>
function c_recipeList(): C_Recipe[] {
  let out: C_Recipe[] = [];
  out.push({name: "Garlic Butter Pasta", ingredients: "pasta|garlic|butter|parmesan|salt", steps: "Boil the pasta in salted water. Melt butter with sliced garlic. Toss the drained pasta in the garlic butter and finish with grated parmesan."});
  out.push({name: "Tomato Egg Scramble", ingredients: "eggs|tomato|onion|oil|salt", steps: "Beat the eggs. Soften onion in oil, add chopped tomato and cook down. Pour in the eggs and stir gently until just set."});
  out.push({name: "Chickpea Salad", ingredients: "chickpeas|tomato|cucumber|lemon|olive oil", steps: "Drain the chickpeas. Dice tomato and cucumber. Toss everything with lemon juice, olive oil and a pinch of salt."});
  out.push({name: "Cheese Omelette", ingredients: "eggs|cheese|butter|milk|pepper", steps: "Whisk eggs with milk and pepper. Melt butter in a pan, pour in the eggs, scatter cheese and fold when nearly set."});
  out.push({name: "Rice and Beans", ingredients: "rice|beans|onion|garlic|cumin", steps: "Cook the rice. Fry onion and garlic with cumin, add the beans and a splash of water, then serve over the rice."});
  out.push({name: "Simple Pancakes", ingredients: "flour|milk|eggs|sugar|butter", steps: "Whisk flour, milk, eggs and sugar into a smooth batter. Cook ladlefuls in a buttered pan until golden on both sides."});
  return out;
}

function c_hasIngredient(state: AppState, name: string): boolean {
  let want: string = strings.toLowerCase(strings.trim(name));
  for (let e: LogEntry of state.entries) {
    if (strings.toLowerCase(strings.trim(e.ingredient)) === want) { return true; }
  }
  return false;
}

function c_ingredientCount(recipe: C_Recipe): number {
  let parts: string[] = strings.split(recipe.ingredients, "|");
  return parts.length();
}

function c_haveCount(state: AppState, recipe: C_Recipe): number {
  let parts: string[] = strings.split(recipe.ingredients, "|");
  let have: number = 0;
  for (let p: string of parts) {
    if (c_hasIngredient(state, p)) { have = have + 1; }
  }
  return have;
}

function c_missingCount(state: AppState, recipe: C_Recipe): number {
  let m: number = c_ingredientCount(recipe) - c_haveCount(state, recipe);
  if (m < 0) { return 0; }
  return m;
}

function c_canCook(state: AppState, recipe: C_Recipe): number {
  if (c_missingCount(state, recipe) <= state.maxMissing) { return 1; }
  return 0;
}

function c_missingList(state: AppState, recipe: C_Recipe): string {
  let parts: string[] = strings.split(recipe.ingredients, "|");
  let text: string = "";
  for (let p: string of parts) {
    if (!c_hasIngredient(state, p)) {
      if (text === "") {
        text = strings.trim(p);
      } else {
        text = text + ", " + strings.trim(p);
      }
    }
  }
  if (text === "") { return "Nothing missing."; }
  return "Missing: " + text;
}

function c_sortedRecipes(state: AppState): C_Recipe[] {
  let all: C_Recipe[] = c_recipeList();
  let out: C_Recipe[] = [];
  let i: number = 0;
  while (i < all.length()) {
    if (c_canCook(state, all[i]) === 1) { out.push(all[i]); }
    i = i + 1;
  }
  i = 0;
  while (i < all.length()) {
    if (c_canCook(state, all[i]) === 0) { out.push(all[i]); }
    i = i + 1;
  }
  return out;
}

function c_selectRecipe(state: AppState, value: number): AppState {
  if (state.c_selected === value) {
    return {c_selected: -1__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  return {c_selected: value__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_addMissing(state: AppState, value: number): AppState {
  let recipes: C_Recipe[] = c_sortedRecipes(state);
  if (value < 0 || value >= recipes.length()) {
    return {c_selected: state.c_selected__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  let recipe: C_Recipe = recipes[value];
  let parts: string[] = strings.split(recipe.ingredients, "|");
  let out: LogEntry[] = [];
  for (let e: LogEntry of state.entries) { out.push(e); }
  let minute: number = time.hourOfDay() * 60 + time.minuteOfHour();
  for (let p: string of parts) {
    if (!c_hasIngredient(state, p)) {
      out.push({ingredient: strings.trim(p), minute: minute});
    }
  }
  return {entries: out__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

{
  let recipes: C_Recipe[] = c_sortedRecipes(state);

    ]));
  }
  let ready: number = 0;
  let i: number = 0;
  while (i < recipes.length()) {
    if (c_canCook(state, recipes[i]) === 1) { ready = ready + 1; }
    i = i + 1;
  }
  let rows: ui.View[] = [];
  i = 0;
  while (i < recipes.length()) {
    let r: C_Recipe = recipes[i];
    let need: number = c_ingredientCount(r);
    let have: number = c_haveCount(state, r);
    let missing: number = c_missingCount(state, r);
    let can: number = c_canCook(state, r);
    let trailer: string = ui.numberToString(missing) + " missing";
    if (can === 1) { trailer = "Can cook now"; }
    let sub: string = ui.numberToString(have) + " of " + ui.numberToString(need) + " ingredients on hand";
    rows.push(ui.ListItem("default", r.name, sub, trailer, "c_selectRecipe", i, true, "list"));
    if (state.c_selected === i) {
      let canWord: string = "No";
      if (can === 1) { canWord = "Yes"; }
      let detail: ui.View[] = [];
      detail.push(ui.KeyValueGroup("default", 2, [
        ui.KeyValueItem("default", "Still missing", ui.numberToString(missing), "ingredients you do not have"),
        ui.KeyValueItem("default", "Can cook now", canWord, "allows up to " + ui.numberToString(state.maxMissing) + " missing")
      ]));
      detail.push(ui.Text("caption", c_missingList(state, r)));
      detail.push(ui.Text("body", r.steps));
      if (missing > 0) {
        detail.push(ui.ActionBar("end", [
          ui.Button("secondary", "Add missing to pantry", "c_addMissing", i, true)
        ]));
      }
      rows.push(ui.Card("surface", [ui.Column("default", detail)]));
    }
    i = i + 1;
  }
  sections.push(ui.Section("content", "", "", [
    ui.SectionHeader("default", "Recipes", "Ready to cook first, then the rest", ui.numberToString(ready) + " of " + ui.numberToString(recipes.length()) + " ready"),
    ui.Column("default", rows)
  ]));
}

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:
    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
      sdk.call("Vera.Ask.text", ["prompt", "Two quick dinners using: " + names + ". One line each.", "maxWords", "60"], "onSuggested");
      return {c_ideas: "Thinking..."__PASSTHROUGH__};
    }
    function onSuggested(state: AppState, value: string): AppState { return {c_ideas: value__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  An answer starting with "error" is shown as a failure the person can try again. Call it only from a button's handler, never from view() or a ticker; and never for numbers the app works out itself or for anything known when the app is made.

Request: recipes filtered by ingredients on hand

The section must do:
- A starter list of recipes, each with its name, the ingredients it needs, and short steps to cook it. The person browses the list, taps a recipe to read its steps, and the phone shows each recipe with how many of its ingredients they already have and marks the ones they can cook now.
- the figure "Still missing": how many ingredients the chosen recipe needs that the person does not have (the plan works it out as max(0, recipeIngredientCount - haveCount); for recipeIngredientCount = 7, haveCount = 6 that is 1)
- the figure "Can cook now": 1 when the recipe needs no more missing items than the person allows, 0 otherwise (a yes or a no worked out as 1 or 0: show it as Yes or No, or as words that say which, never as the number) (the plan works it out as missingCount <= maxMissing; for missingCount = 1, maxMissing = 2 that is 1)

The person sets these on the screen and nothing else uses them yet; the section uses them:
- "Max missing items": state.maxMissing

The program already has these: use them, do not make your own:
- a list of entries: state.entries is LogEntry[] with the fields {ingredient: string, minute: number}. Its form, its Add and Remove buttons and its rows are already on the screen. The section makes no list of its own for the same entries; to add one it copies state.entries into a new array, pushes a LogEntry (minute: time.hourOfDay() * 60 + time.minuteOfHour()) and returns {entries: thatArray __PASSTHROUGH__}.

Nothing they show is shown again: no second list, total, chart, Remove last or Start over button. While what the section works from is still empty, it shows one plain line saying what will appear and when, never a ui.EmptyState: the list above already has one (two empty states one under the other read as a broken screen).

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:
    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {

A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.

function c_parseDate(s: string): number {
  let t: string = strings.trim(s);
  if (strings.length(t) === 0) { return -1; }
  let y: number = -1;
  let m: number = -1;
  let d: number = -1;
  if (strings.contains(t, "-")) {
    let parts: string[] = strings.split(t, "-");
    if (parts.length() !== 3) { return -1; }
    y = strings.toNumber(parts[0], -1);
    m = strings.toNumber(parts[1], -1);
    d = strings.toNumber(parts[2], -1);
  } else {
    if (strings.length(t) !== 8) { return -1; }
    y = strings.toNumber(strings.substring(t, 0, 4), -1);
    m = strings.toNumber(strings.substring(t, 4, 6), -1);
    d = strings.toNumber(strings.substring(t, 6, 8), -1);
  }
  if (y < 1 || m < 1 || m > 12 || d < 1 || d > 31) { return -1; }
  let days: number = 0;
  let yy: number = 1970;
  while (yy < y) {
    if ((yy % 4 === 0 && yy % 100 !== 0) || yy % 400 === 0) { days = days + 366; } else { days = days + 365; }
    yy = yy + 1;
  }
  let mm: number = 1;
  while (mm < m) {
    if (mm === 2) {
      if ((y % 4 === 0 && y % 100 !== 0) || y % 400 === 0) { days = days + 29; } else { days = days + 28; }
    } else if (mm === 4 || mm === 6 || mm === 9 || mm === 11) {
      days = days + 30;
    } else {
      days = days + 31;
    }
    mm = mm + 1;
  }
  days = days + d - 1;
  return days;
}

function c_gap(state: AppState): number {
  let a: number = c_parseDate(state.startDate);
  let b: number = c_parseDate(state.endDate);
  if (a < 0 || b < 0) { return -1; }
  return math.abs(b - a);
}

function c_weeks(gap: number): number {
  return math.floor(gap / 7);
}

function c_weekDays(gap: number): number {
  return gap % 7;
}

function c_months(gap: number): number {
  return math.floor(gap / 30);
}

function c_monthDays(gap: number): number {
  return gap % 30;
}
</functions>

    let months: number = c_months(gap);
    let monthDays: number = c_monthDays(gap);
    body.push(ui.MetricGroup("default", 3, [
      ui.NumberStat("accent", "Days", gap, "", "", 1, "from " + state.startDate + " to " + state.endDate, "calendar"),

function daysInMonth(month: number, year: number): number {
  if (month === 2) {
    if (year % 4 === 0) {
      if (year % 100 === 0) {
        if (year % 400 === 0) { return 29; }
        return 28;
      }
      return 29;
    }

  }
  if (month === 4 || month === 6 || month === 9 || month === 11) { return 30; }
  return 31;
}

function dayOfYear(month: number, day: number, year: number): number {
  let total: number = 0;
  let m: number = 1;
  while (m < month) {
    total = total + daysInMonth(m, year);
    m = m + 1;
  }
  return total + day;
}

function weeksUntilBirthday(state: AppState): number {
  let month: number = math.floor(strings.toNumber(state.birthdayMonthText, 1));
  let day: number = math.floor(strings.toNumber(state.birthdayDayText, 1));
  if (month < 1) { month = 1; }
  if (month > 12) { month = 12; }
  let maxDay: number = daysInMonth(month, time.year());
  if (day < 1) { day = 1; }
  if (day > maxDay) { day = maxDay; }
  let today: number = dayOfYear(time.monthOfYear(), time.dayOfMonth(), time.year());
  let target: number = dayOfYear(month, day, time.year());
  let diff: number = target - today;
  if (diff < 0) {
    diff = diff + 365;
    if (daysInMonth(2, time.year()) === 29) { diff = diff + 1; }
  }
  return math.floor(diff / 7);
}

function c_parseDay(s: string): number {
  let t: string = strings.trim(s);
  if (strings.length(t) === 0) { return 0; }
  let parts: string[] = strings.split(t, "-");
  if (parts.length() !== 3) { return 0; }
  let y: number = strings.toNumber(parts[0], 0);
  let m: number = strings.toNumber(parts[1], 0);
  let d: number = strings.toNumber(parts[2], 0);
  if (y < 1 || m < 1 || m > 12 || d < 1 || d > 31) { return 0; }
  let yy: number = y;
  let mm: number = m;
  if (mm <= 2) { yy = yy - 1; }
  let era: number = math.floor(yy / 400);
  let yoe: number = yy - era * 400;
  let mp: number = mm + 9;
  if (mm > 2) { mp = mm - 3; }
  let doy: number = math.floor((153 * mp + 2) / 5) + d - 1;
  let doe: number = yoe * 365 + math.floor(yoe / 4) - math.floor(yoe / 100) + doy;
  return era * 146097 + doe - 719468;
}

function c_daysApart(state: AppState): number {
  let a: number = c_parseDay(state.startDate);
  let b: number = c_parseDay(state.endDate);
  return b - a;
}

function c_weeksBetween(state: AppState): number {
  let days: number = c_daysApart(state);
  let w: number = math.floor(days / 7);
  if (w < 0) { return -math.floor(-days / 7); }
  return w;
}

function c_leftoverDays(state: AppState): number {
  let days: number = c_daysApart(state);
  let w: number = c_weeksBetween(state);
  return days - w * 7;
}

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:

Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>

</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:
    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
      sdk.call("Vera.Ask.text", ["prompt", "Two quick dinners using: " + names + ". One line each.", "maxWords", "60"], "onSuggested");
      return {c_ideas: "Thinking..."__PASSTHROUGH__};
    }
    function onSuggested(state: AppState, value: string): AppState { return {c_ideas: value__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  An answer starting with "error" is shown as a failure the person can try again. Call it only from a button's handler, never from view() or a ticker; and never for numbers the app works out itself or for anything known when the app is made.

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:
    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
      sdk.call("Vera.Ask.text", ["prompt", "Two quick dinners using: " + names + ". One line each.", "maxWords", "60"], "onSuggested");
      return {c_ideas: "Thinking..."__PASSTHROUGH__};
    }
    function onSuggested(state: AppState, value: string): AppState { return {c_ideas: value__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  An answer starting with "error" is shown as a failure the person can try again. Call it only from a button's handler, never from view() or a ticker; and never for numbers the app works out itself or for anything known when the app is made.

  deck.push({term: "Nucleus", definition: "The control centre of the cell that holds the DNA.", missed: false, seen: false});
  deck.push({term: "Chloroplast", definition: "The organelle in plant cells where photosynthesis happens.", missed: false, seen: false});
  deck.push({term: "Osmosis", definition: "The movement of water across a membrane from high to low water concentration.", missed: false, seen: false});
  deck.push({term: "Diffusion", definition: "The spreading of particles from high to low concentration.", missed: false, seen: false});
  deck.push({term: "Mitosis", definition: "Cell division that makes two identical body cells.", missed: false, seen: false});
  deck.push({term: "Meiosis", definition: "Cell division that makes sex cells with half the chromosomes.", missed: false, seen: false});
  deck.push({term: "Enzyme", definition: "A protein that speeds up a reaction in the body.", missed: false, seen: false});
  deck.push({term: "Photosynthesis", definition: "How plants use light, water and carbon dioxide to make glucose.", missed: false, seen: false});
  deck.push({term: "DNA", definition: "The molecule that carries genetic instructions.", missed: false, seen: false});
  deck.push({term: "RNA", definition: "A molecule that carries instructions from DNA to the ribosome.", missed: false, seen: false});
  deck.push({term: "Protein synthesis", definition: "The building of proteins from amino acids at the ribosome.", missed: false, seen: false});
  deck.push({term: "Homeostasis", definition: "Keeping the body's internal conditions steady.", missed: false, seen: false});
  deck.push({term: "Natural selection", definition: "Organisms best suited to their environment survive and pass on their traits.", missed: false, seen: false});
  return deck;
}

function c_flip(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  return {c_flipped: !state.c_flipped, c_flipTrigger: state.c_flipTrigger + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_mark(state: AppState, value: number): AppState {
  let out: C_Card[] = [];
  let i: number = 0;
  while (i < state.c_cards.length()) {
    let c: C_Card = state.c_cards[i];
    if (i === state.c_index) {
      let missed: boolean = false;
      if (value === 1) { missed = true; }
      out.push({term: c.term, definition: c.definition, missed: missed, seen: true});
    } else {
      out.push(c);
    }
    i = i + 1;
  }
  let next: number = state.c_index + 1;
  if (next >= out.length()) { next = 0; }
  return {c_cards: out, c_index: next, c_flipped: false, c_flipTrigger: state.c_flipTrigger + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_next(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  let next: number = state.c_index + 1;
  if (next >= state.c_cards.length()) { next = 0; }
  return {c_index: next, c_flipped: false, c_flipTrigger: state.c_flipTrigger + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_prev(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  let prev: number = state.c_index - 1;
  if (prev < 0) { prev = state.c_cards.length() - 1; }
  return {c_index: prev, c_flipped: false, c_flipTrigger: state.c_flipTrigger + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_startReview(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  let first: number = -1;
  let i: number = 0;
  while (i < state.c_cards.length()) {
    if (state.c_cards[i].missed && first < 0) { first = i; }
    i = i + 1;
  }
  if (first < 0) { first = 0; }
  return {c_reviewMode: true, c_index: first, c_flipped: false, c_flipTrigger: state.c_flipTrigger + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_endReview(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  return {c_reviewMode: false, c_index: 0, c_flipped: false, c_flipTrigger: state.c_flipTrigger + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_clearMissed(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  let out: C_Card[] = [];
  for (let c: C_Card of state.c_cards) {
    out.push({term: c.term, definition: c.definition, missed: false, seen: c.seen});
  }
  return {c_cards: out, c_reviewMode: false, c_index: 0, c_flipped: false, c_flipTrigger: state.c_flipTrigger + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_shuffle(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  let deck: C_Card[] = [];
  if (state.c_cards.length() === 0) {
    deck = c_buildDeck();
  } else {
    for (let c: C_Card of state.c_cards) {
      deck.push(c);
    }
  }
  let seed: number = state.c_shuffleSeed + 1;
  let n: number = deck.length();
  let i: number = n - 1;
  while (i > 0) {
    seed = math.randomStep(seed);
    let j: number = math.randomBelow(seed, i + 1);
    let tmp: C_Card = deck[i];
    deck[i] = deck[j];
    deck[j] = tmp;
    i = i - 1;
  }
  return {c_cards: deck, c_index: 0, c_flipped: false, c_flipTrigger: state.c_flipTrigger + 1, c_shuffleSeed: seed__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.

Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>

Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion.
