- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. - Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.

- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.

- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.

Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:
    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
      sdk.call("Vera.Ask.text", ["prompt", "Two quick dinners using: " + names + ". One line each.", "maxWords", "60"], "onSuggested");
      return {c_ideas: "Thinking..."__PASSTHROUGH__};
    }
    function onSuggested(state: AppState, value: string): AppState { return {c_ideas: value__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  An answer starting with "error" is shown as a failure the person can try again. Call it only from a button's handler, never from view() or a ticker; and never for numbers the app works out itself or for anything known when the app is made.

<classes>

c_lastBuzzMinute: number = -1
c_buzzCount: number = 0
</fields>
<functions>
function c_intervalMinutes(state: AppState): number {
  let values: number[] = [30, 45, 60, 90, 120];
  let i: number = state.reminderIntervalIndex;
  if (i < 0 || i > 4) { return 60; }
  return values[i];
}

function c_buzzNow(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  sdk.call("SensorServiceKit.vibrator.vibrate", ["duration", "800"], "c_onBuzzAnswer");
  return {c_buzzStatus: "Buzzing now...", c_lastBuzzMinute: time.hourOfDay() * 60 + time.minuteOfHour(), c_buzzCount: state.c_buzzCount + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_onBuzzAnswer(state: AppState, value: string): AppState {
  let failed: boolean = strings.startsWith(value, "declined") || strings.startsWith(value, "error");
  if (failed) {
    return {c_buzzStatus: "The buzz did not go through: " + value__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  return {c_buzzStatus: "Buzzed at " + ui.clockToString(time.hourOfDay() * 60 + time.minuteOfHour())__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_onTick(state: AppState, elapsedMs: number): AppState {
  let nowMinute: number = time.hourOfDay() * 60 + time.minuteOfHour();
  let interval: number = c_intervalMinutes(state);
  let due: boolean = false;
  if (nowMinute >= state.startTime) {
    if (state.c_lastBuzzMinute < 0) {
      due = true;
    } else {
      if (nowMinute - state.c_lastBuzzMinute >= interval) {
        due = true;
      }
    }
  }
  if (!due) {
    return {__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  sdk.call("SensorServiceKit.vibrator.vibrate", ["duration", "800"], "c_onBuzzAnswer");
  return {c_lastBuzzMinute: nowMinute, c_buzzStatus: "Buzzing now...", c_buzzCount: state.c_buzzCount + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
}
</functions>

  }
  let c_rows: ui.View[] = [];
  c_rows.push(ui.KeyValueGroup("default", 2, [
    ui.KeyValueItem("default", "Every", ui.numberToString(c_interval) + " minutes", "while you are awake"),
    ui.KeyValueItem("default", "Next buzz", ui.clockToString(c_nextMinute), "from your start time"),
    ui.KeyValueItem("default", "Buzzes so far", ui.numberToString(state.c_buzzCount), "this session")
  ]));
  c_rows.push(ui.Ticker("default", "c_waterBuzz", 20000, true, "c_onTick"));
  c_rows.push(ui.ActionBar("end", [
    ui.Button("primary", "Buzz me now", "c_buzzNow", 0, true)
  ]));
  if (state.c_buzzStatus !== "") {
    c_rows.push(ui.InsetBanner("default", "Last buzz", state.c_buzzStatus, "", "", "info"));
  }
  sections.push(ui.Section("content", "Reminder buzz", "The phone buzzes on this schedule while the app is open", c_rows));
}

Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:
    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
      sdk.call("Vera.Ask.text", ["prompt", "Two quick dinners using: " + names + ". One line each.", "maxWords", "60"], "onSuggested");
      return {c_ideas: "Thinking..."__PASSTHROUGH__};
    }
    function onSuggested(state: AppState, value: string): AppState { return {c_ideas: value__PASSTHROUGH__}; }

<classes>

</classes>
<fields>
c_lastBuzz: number = 0
c_buzzCount: number = 0
c_status: string = ""
</fields>
<functions>
function c_buzz(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  sdk.call("SensorServiceKit.vibrator.vibrate", ["duration", "800"], "c_onBuzz");
  return {c_status: "Vibrating now - time to stretch."__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_onBuzz(state: AppState, value: string): AppState {
  let failed: boolean = strings.startsWith(value, "declined") || strings.startsWith(value, "error");
  if (failed) {
    return {c_status: "The phone could not vibrate: " + value__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  return {c_status: "Buzzed - time to stretch."__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_tick(state: AppState, elapsedMs: number): AppState {
  let nowMinute: number = time.hourOfDay() * 60 + time.minuteOfHour();
  let start: number = state.startTime;
  let end: number = state.endTime;
  let inWindow: boolean = false;
  if (start <= end) {
    inWindow = nowMinute >= start && nowMinute < end;
  } else {
    inWindow = nowMinute >= start || nowMinute < end;
  }
  if (!inWindow) {
    return {__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  let last: number = state.c_lastBuzz;
  let due: boolean = false;
  if (last === 0) {
    due = true;
  } else {
    let gap: number = nowMinute - last;
    if (gap < 0) {
      gap = gap + 1440;
    }
    due = gap >= 60;
  }
  if (!due) {
    return {__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  sdk.call("SensorServiceKit.vibrator.vibrate", ["duration", "800"], "c_onBuzz");
  return {c_lastBuzz: nowMinute, c_buzzCount: state.c_buzzCount + 1, c_status: "Buzzed - time to stretch."__PASSTHROUGH__};
}
</functions>
<view>
{

  let c_start: number = state.startTime;
  let c_end: number = state.endTime;
  let c_inWindow: boolean = false;
  if (c_start <= c_end) {
    c_inWindow = c_nowMinute >= c_start && c_nowMinute < c_end;
  } else {
    c_inWindow = c_nowMinute >= c_start || c_nowMinute < c_end;
  }
  let c_next: number = c_nowMinute - (c_nowMinute % 60) + 60;
  if (c_next >= 1440) {
    c_next = c_next - 1440;
  }
  let c_minsToNext: number = c_next - c_nowMinute;
  if (c_minsToNext < 0) {
    c_minsToNext = c_minsToNext + 1440;
  }
  let c_rows: ui.View[] = [];
  c_rows.push(ui.KeyValueItem("default", "Reminder window", ui.clockToString(c_start) + " - " + ui.clockToString(c_end), "A buzz every hour inside this window"));
  c_rows.push(ui.KeyValueItem("default", "Next buzz", ui.clockToString(c_next), "On the hour"));
  c_rows.push(ui.KeyValueItem("default", "Buzzes so far", ui.numberToString(state.c_buzzCount), ""));
  let c_body: ui.View[] = [];
  c_body.push(ui.Ticker("default", "c_stretchTicker", 30000, true, "c_tick"));
  if (c_inWindow) {
    c_body.push(ui.InsetBanner("success", "Reminders running", "The phone will buzz every hour until " + ui.clockToString(c_end) + ".", "", "", "check"));
  } else {
    c_body.push(ui.InsetBanner("default", "Outside the window", "Reminders pause until " + ui.clockToString(c_start) + ".", "", "", "clock"));
  }
  c_body.push(ui.NumberStat("accent", "Minutes until next buzz", c_minsToNext, "", " min", 1, "Next buzz at " + ui.clockToString(c_next), "clock"));
  c_body.push(ui.KeyValueGroup("default", 1, c_rows));
  if (state.c_status !== "") {
    c_body.push(ui.Text("caption", state.c_status));
  }
  c_body.push(ui.ActionBar("end", [
    ui.Button("primary", "Buzz now", "c_buzz", 0, true)
  ]));
  sections.push(ui.Section("content", "Stretch reminders", "Vibrates every hour between your start and end time", c_body));
}
</view>

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:
    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
      sdk.call("Vera.Ask.text", ["prompt", "Two quick dinners using: " + names + ". One line each.", "maxWords", "60"], "onSuggested");
      return {c_ideas: "Thinking..."__PASSTHROUGH__};
    }
    function onSuggested(state: AppState, value: string): AppState { return {c_ideas: value__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  An answer starting with "error" is shown as a failure the person can try again. Call it only from a button's handler, never from view() or a ticker; and never for numbers the app works out itself or for anything known when the app is made.

<functions>
function c_buildQuiz(count: number, seed: number): C_Question[] {
  let prompts: string[] = [];
  let answers: string[] = [];
  let facts: string[] = [];
  prompts.push("Who was the first president of the United States?");
  answers.push("George Washington");
  facts.push("Washington served from 1789 to 1797.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 16th president, who led the Union through the Civil War?");
  answers.push("Abraham Lincoln");

  answers.push("Thomas Jefferson");
  facts.push("The Louisiana Purchase doubled the size of the country in 1803.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 32nd president and led the country through most of World War II?");
  answers.push("Franklin D. Roosevelt");
  facts.push("FDR was elected four times, the only president to do so.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 35th president and set the goal of reaching the Moon?");
  answers.push("John F. Kennedy");
  facts.push("Kennedy announced the Moon goal in 1961.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 40th president and asked Gorbachev to tear down the Berlin Wall?");
  answers.push("Ronald Reagan");
  facts.push("Reagan served two terms, from 1981 to 1989.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 1st president to live in the White House?");
  answers.push("John Adams");
  facts.push("John Adams moved into the White House in 1800.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 28th president and led the country during World War I?");
  answers.push("Woodrow Wilson");
  facts.push("Wilson helped found the League of Nations.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 44th president and the first African American to hold the office?");
  answers.push("Barack Obama");
  facts.push("Obama served from 2009 to 2017.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 18th president and commanded the Union Army at the end of the Civil War?");
  answers.push("Ulysses S. Grant");
  facts.push("Grant accepted Lee's surrender at Appomattox in 1865.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 26th president and championed the national parks?");
  answers.push("Theodore Roosevelt");
  facts.push("Theodore Roosevelt created the U.S. Forest Service.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 33rd president and ordered the use of atomic bombs in 1945?");
  answers.push("Harry S. Truman");
  facts.push("Truman took office in April 1945.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 34th president and Supreme Allied Commander in Europe?");
  answers.push("Dwight D. Eisenhower");
  facts.push("Eisenhower launched the interstate highway system.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 39th president and brokered the Camp David Accords?");
  answers.push("Jimmy Carter");
  facts.push("The Camp David Accords were signed in 1978.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 42nd president and signed the North American Free Trade Agreement?");
  answers.push("Bill Clinton");
  facts.push("Clinton served from 1993 to 2001.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 41st president and led the coalition in the Gulf War?");
  answers.push("George H. W. Bush");
  facts.push("Bush served one term, from 1989 to 1993.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 2nd president and the first to live in the White House?");
  answers.push("John Adams");
  facts.push("John Adams was the first president to occupy the White House.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 4th president and is called the Father of the Constitution?");
  answers.push("James Madison");
  facts.push("Madison helped draft the Constitution in 1787.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 5th president and issued the Monroe Doctrine?");
  answers.push("James Monroe");
  facts.push("The Monroe Doctrine was declared in 1823.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 7th president and won the Battle of New Orleans?");
  answers.push("Andrew Jackson");
  facts.push("Jackson served from 1829 to 1837.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 11th president and oversaw the Mexican-American War?");
  answers.push("James K. Polk");
  facts.push("Polk served one term, from 1845 to 1849.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 19th president and ended Reconstruction?");
  answers.push("Rutherford B. Hayes");
  facts.push("Hayes served from 1877 to 1881.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 27th president and later became Chief Justice?");
  answers.push("William Howard Taft");
  facts.push("Taft served as Chief Justice from 1921 to 1930.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 36th president and signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964?");
  answers.push("Lyndon B. Johnson");
  facts.push("Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act in 1965.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 37th president and opened relations with China?");
  answers.push("Richard Nixon");
  facts.push("Nixon visited China in 1972.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 38th president and pardoned his predecessor?");
  answers.push("Gerald Ford");
  facts.push("Ford took office in 1974.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 43rd president and led the response to the September 11 attacks?");
  answers.push("George W. Bush");
  facts.push("Bush served from 2001 to 2009.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 45th president?");
  answers.push("Donald Trump");
  facts.push("Trump served from 2017 to 2021.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 46th president?");
  answers.push("Joe Biden");
  facts.push("Biden took office in January 2021.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 6th president and the son of a president?");
  answers.push("John Quincy Adams");
  facts.push("John Quincy Adams served from 1825 to 1829.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 8th president and the first born a U.S. citizen?");
  answers.push("Martin Van Buren");
  facts.push("Van Buren served from 1837 to 1841.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 9th president and served only one month in office?");
  answers.push("William Henry Harrison");
  facts.push("Harrison died in 1841, 31 days after taking office.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 10th president and became president after Harrison's death?");
  answers.push("John Tyler");
  facts.push("Tyler served from 1841 to 1845.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 12th president and died in office in 1850?");
  answers.push("Zachary Taylor");
  facts.push("Taylor served from 1849 to 1850.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 13th president and signed the Compromise of 1850?");
  answers.push("Millard Fillmore");
  facts.push("Fillmore served from 1850 to 1853.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 14th president and signed the Kansas-Nebraska Act?");
  answers.push("Franklin Pierce");
  facts.push("Pierce served from 1853 to 1857.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 15th president and served just before the Civil War?");
  answers.push("James Buchanan");
  facts.push("Buchanan served from 1857 to 1861.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 17th president and became president after Lincoln's death?");
  answers.push("Andrew Johnson");
  facts.push("Johnson served from 1865 to 1869.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 20th president and was shot in 1881?");
  answers.push("James A. Garfield");
  facts.push("Garfield served only six months in 1881.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 21st president and became president after Garfield's death?");
  answers.push("Chester A. Arthur");
  facts.push("Arthur served from 1881 to 1885.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 22nd and 24th president, serving two non-consecutive terms?");
  answers.push("Grover Cleveland");
  facts.push("Cleveland served 1885-1889 and 1893-1897.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 23rd president?");
  answers.push("Benjamin Harrison");
  facts.push("Harrison served from 1889 to 1893.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 25th president and was shot in 1901?");
  answers.push("William McKinley");
  facts.push("McKinley served from 1897 to 1901.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 29th president and died in office in 1923?");
  answers.push("Warren G. Harding");
  facts.push("Harding served from 1921 to 1923.");
  prompts.push("Who was the 30th president and became president after Harding's death?");
  answers.push("Calvin Coolidge");
  facts.push("Coolidge served from 1923 to 1929.");

  answers.push("Herbert Hoover");
  facts.push("Hoover served from 1929 to 1933.");
  let total: number = prompts.length();
  let order: number[] = [];
  let i: number = 0;
  while (i < total) {
    order.push(i);
    i = i + 1;
  }
  let s: number = seed;
  let j: number = total - 1;
  while (j > 0) {
    s = math.randomStep(s);
    let k: number = math.randomBelow(s, j + 1);
    let tmp: number = order[j];
    order[j] = order[k];
    order[k] = tmp;
    j = j - 1;
  }
  let out: C_Question[] = [];
  let n: number = 0;
  while (n < count && n < total) {
    let idx: number = order[n];
    let correctName: string = answers[idx];
    let opts: string[] = [];
    opts.push(correctName);
    let guard: number = 0;
    while (opts.length() < 4 && guard < 200) {
      s = math.randomStep(s);
      let pick: number = math.randomBelow(s, total);
      let cand: string = answers[pick];
      let dup: boolean = false;
      for (let o: string of opts) {
        if (o === cand) { dup = true; }
      }
      if (!dup) { opts.push(cand); }
      guard = guard + 1;
    }
    let m: number = opts.length() - 1;
    while (m > 0) {
      s = math.randomStep(s);
      let q: number = math.randomBelow(s, m + 1);
      let t2: string = opts[m];
      opts[m] = opts[q];
      opts[q] = t2;
      m = m - 1;
    }
    let correctIndex: number = 0;
    let c: number = 0;
    while (c < opts.length()) {
      if (opts[c] === correctName) { correctIndex = c; }
      c = c + 1;
    }
    out.push({prompt: prompts[idx], choices: opts, correct: correctIndex, fact: facts[idx]});
    n = n + 1;
  }
  return out;
}

function c_start(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  let seed: number = state.c_seed + 1;
  let quiz: C_Question[] = c_buildQuiz(state.questionCount, seed);
  return {c_quiz: quiz, c_index: 0, c_score: 0, c_answered: false, c_picked: -1, c_finished: false, c_started: true, c_seed: seed, c_streak: 0, c_bestStreak: 0__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_answer(state: AppState, value: number): AppState {
  if (state.c_answered || state.c_finished) {
    return {__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  let total: number = state.c_quiz.length();
  if (state.c_index >= total) {
    return {__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  let q: C_Question = state.c_quiz[state.c_index];
  let gained: number = 0;
  if (value === q.correct) { gained = 1; }
  let streak: number = state.c_streak;
  let best: number = state.c_bestStreak;
  if (gained === 1) {
    streak = streak + 1;
    if (streak > best) { best = streak; }
  } else {
    streak = 0;
  }
  return {c_answered: true, c_picked: value, c_score: state.c_score + gained, c_streak: streak, c_bestStreak: best__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_next(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  if (!state.c_answered) {
    return {__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  let total: number = state.c_quiz.length();
  let nextIndex: number = state.c_index + 1;
  if (nextIndex >= total) {
    return {c_finished: true, c_answered: false, c_picked: -1__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  return {c_index: nextIndex, c_answered: false, c_picked: -1__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_restart(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  return {c_started: false, c_finished: false, c_answered: false, c_picked: -1, c_index: 0, c_score: 0, c_streak: 0, c_bestStreak: 0__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

        ]));

      ]));

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:
    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
      sdk.call("Vera.Ask.text", ["prompt", "Two quick dinners using: " + names + ". One line each.", "maxWords", "60"], "onSuggested");
      return {c_ideas: "Thinking..."__PASSTHROUGH__};
    }
    function onSuggested(state: AppState, value: string): AppState { return {c_ideas: value__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  An answer starting with "error" is shown as a failure the person can try again. Call it only from a button's handler, never from view() or a ticker; and never for numbers the app works out itself or for anything known when the app is made.

  let total: number = prompts.length();

  while (i < total) {
    order.push(i);
    i = i + 1;
  }
  let s: number = seed;
  let j: number = total - 1;
  while (j > 0) {
    s = math.randomStep(s);
    let k: number = math.randomBelow(s, j + 1);
    let tmp: number = order[j];
    order[j] = order[k];
    order[k] = tmp;
    j = j - 1;
  }
  let out: C_Question[] = [];
  let n: number = 0;
  while (n < count && n < total) {
    let idx: number = order[n];
    let correctName: string = answers[idx];
    let opts: string[] = [];
    opts.push(correctName);
    let guard: number = 0;
    while (opts.length() < 4 && guard < 200) {
      s = math.randomStep(s);
      let pick: number = math.randomBelow(s, total);
      let cand: string = answers[pick];
      let dup: boolean = false;
      for (let o: string of opts) {
        if (o === cand) { dup = true; }
      }
      if (!dup) { opts.push(cand); }
      guard = guard + 1;
    }
    let m: number = opts.length() - 1;
    while (m > 0) {
      s = math.randomStep(s);
      let q: number = math.randomBelow(s, m + 1);
      let t2: string = opts[m];
      opts[m] = opts[q];
      opts[q] = t2;
      m = m - 1;

    let correctIndex: number = 0;
    let c: number = 0;

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:
    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
      sdk.call("Vera.Ask.text", ["prompt", "Two quick dinners using: " + names + ". One line each.", "maxWords", "60"], "onSuggested");
      return {c_ideas: "Thinking..."__PASSTHROUGH__};
    }
    function onSuggested(state: AppState, value: string): AppState { return {c_ideas: value__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  An answer starting with "error" is shown as a failure the person can try again. Call it only from a button's handler, never from view() or a ticker; and never for numbers the app works out itself or for anything known when the app is made.

function c_start(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {

function c_answer(state: AppState, value: number): AppState {
  if (state.c_answered || state.c_finished) {
    return {__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  let total: number = state.c_quiz.length();
  if (state.c_index >= total) {

  }
  let q: C_Question = state.c_quiz[state.c_index];

  return {c_index: nextIndex, c_answered: false, c_picked: -1__PASSTHROUGH__};

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:
    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
      sdk.call("Vera.Ask.text", ["prompt", "Two quick dinners using: " + names + ". One line each.", "maxWords", "60"], "onSuggested");
      return {c_ideas: "Thinking..."__PASSTHROUGH__};
    }
    function onSuggested(state: AppState, value: string): AppState { return {c_ideas: value__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  An answer starting with "error" is shown as a failure the person can try again. Call it only from a button's handler, never from view() or a ticker; and never for numbers the app works out itself or for anything known when the app is made.

  prompts.push("Who was the 31st president and took office at the start of the Great Depression?");
  answers.push("Herbert Hoover");
  facts.push("Hoover served from 1929 to 1933.");
  let total: number = prompts.length();
  let order: number[] = [];
  let i: number = 0;
  while (i < total) {
    order.push(i);
    i = i + 1;
  }
  let s: number = seed;
  let j: number = total - 1;
  while (j > 0) {
    s = math.randomStep(s);
    let k: number = math.randomBelow(s, j + 1);
    let tmp: number = order[j];
    order[j] = order[k];
    order[k] = tmp;
    j = j - 1;
  }
  let out: C_Question[] = [];
  let n: number = 0;
  while (n < count && n < total) {
    let idx: number = order[n];
    let correctName: string = answers[idx];
    let opts: string[] = [];
    opts.push(correctName);
    let guard: number = 0;
    while (opts.length() < 4 && guard < 200) {
      s = math.randomStep(s);
      let pick: number = math.randomBelow(s, total);
      let cand: string = answers[pick];
      let dup: boolean = false;
      for (let o: string of opts) {
        if (o === cand) { dup = true; }
      }
      if (!dup) { opts.push(cand); }
      guard = guard + 1;
    }
    let m: number = opts.length() - 1;
    while (m > 0) {
      s = math.randomStep(s);
      let q: number = math.randomBelow(s, m + 1);
      let t2: string = opts[m];
      opts[m] = opts[q];
      opts[q] = t2;
      m = m - 1;
    }
    let correctIndex: number = 0;
    let c: number = 0;
    while (c < opts.length()) {
      if (opts[c] === correctName) { correctIndex = c; }
      c = c + 1;
    }
    out.push({prompt: prompts[idx], choices: opts, correct: correctIndex, fact: facts[idx]});
    n = n + 1;
  }
  return out;
}

function c_start(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  let seed: number = state.c_seed + 1;

function c_answer(state: AppState, value: number): AppState {
  if (state.c_answered || state.c_finished) {
    return {__PASSTHROUGH__};

  let total: number = state.c_quiz.length();
  if (state.c_index >= total) {
    return {__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  let q: C_Question = state.c_quiz[state.c_index];
  let gained: number = 0;
  if (value === q.correct) { gained = 1; }
  return {c_answered: true, c_picked: value, c_score: state.c_score + gained__PASSTHROUGH__};

function c_next(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  if (!state.c_answered) {
    return {__PASSTHROUGH__};

  let total: number = state.c_quiz.length();
  let nextIndex: number = state.c_index + 1;
  if (nextIndex >= total) {
    return {c_finished: true, c_answered: false, c_picked: -1__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  return {c_index: nextIndex, c_answered: false, c_picked: -1__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why.
