  q.push({text: "Which album by Pink Floyd features a prism on the cover?", a: "The Wall", b: "Wish You Were Here", c: "The Dark Side of the Moon", d: "Animals", correct: 2, category: "Albums"});
  q.push({text: "Which genre did Bob Marley popularise?", a: "Reggae", b: "Ska", c: "Calypso", d: "Soca", correct: 0, category: "History"});

function c_categories(): string[] {
  let out: string[] = [];
  out.push("All categories");
  out.push("Artists");
  out.push("Albums");
  out.push("Songs");
  out.push("History");
  return out;
}

function c_pickCategory(state: AppState, value: number): AppState {
  let cats: string[] = c_categories();
  let chosen: string = "";
  if (value >= 0 && value < cats.length()) {
    chosen = cats[value];
  }
  return {c_category: chosen__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_shuffle(state: AppState, count: number): number[] {
  let bank: C_Question[] = c_bank();
  let total: number = bank.length();
  let pool: number[] = [];
  let i: number = 0;
  while (i < total) {
    if (state.c_category === "" || state.c_category === "All categories" || bank[i].category === state.c_category) {
      pool.push(i);
    }
    i = i + 1;
  }
  let seed: number = state.c_round * 7919 + count * 104729 + 17;
  let out: number[] = [];
  let n: number = 0;
  while (n < count && pool.length() > 0) {
    seed = math.randomStep(seed);
    let pick: number = math.randomBelow(seed, pool.length());
    let chosen: number = pool[pick];
    let kept: number[] = [];
    let j: number = 0;
    while (j < pool.length()) {
      if (j !== pick) {
        kept.push(pool[j]);
      }
      j = j + 1;
    }
    pool = kept;
    out.push(chosen);
    n = n + 1;
  }
  return out;
}

function c_start(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  let count: number = state.questionCount;
  if (count < 1) { count = 1; }
  if (count > 20) { count = 20; }
  let round: number = state.c_round + 1;
  let order: number[] = c_shuffle(state, count);
  return {c_order: order, c_index: 0, c_correct: 0, c_answered: 0, c_picked: -1, c_finished: false, c_started: true, c_round: round__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_answer(state: AppState, value: number): AppState {
  if (state.c_finished) { return {__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  if (state.c_picked >= 0) { return {__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  let bank: C_Question[] = c_bank();
  let pos: number = state.c_index;
  if (pos < 0 || pos >= state.c_order.length()) { return {__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  let qi: number = state.c_order[pos];
  let q: C_Question = bank[qi];
  let correct: number = state.c_correct;
  if (value === q.correct) {
    correct = correct + 1;
  }
  return {c_picked: value, c_correct: correct, c_answered: state.c_answered + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_next(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  if (state.c_picked < 0) { return {__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  let nextIndex: number = state.c_index + 1;
  if (nextIndex >= state.c_order.length()) {
    return {c_finished: true, c_picked: -1, c_index: nextIndex__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  return {c_index: nextIndex, c_picked: -1__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_restart(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  return c_start(state, 0);
}
</functions>

{

  let score: number = state.c_correct * pointsPerCorrect;
  let progressMax: number = total;
  if (progressMax < 1) { progressMax = 1; }

    let cats: string[] = c_categories();

    if (catLabel === "") {

    }
    body.push(ui.Section("content", "", "", [

      ui.ActionBar("center", [
        ui.Button("primary", "Start round", "c_start", 0, true)
      ])
    ]));
  } else if (state.c_finished) {
    let verdict: string = "Keep practising!";
    if (total > 0 && state.c_correct === total) {
      verdict = "Perfect round!";
    } else if (total > 0 && state.c_correct * 2 >= total) {
      verdict = "Nicely done!";
    }
    body.push(ui.Motion("pop", state.c_round + state.c_correct, [
      ui.Hero("accent", "ROUND COMPLETE", verdict, ui.numberToString(state.c_correct) + " of " + ui.numberToString(total) + " correct", [

      ui.Button("primary", "Play again", "c_restart", 0, true)
    ]));

    let pos: number = state.c_index;

      let qi: number = state.c_order[pos];
      if (qi >= 0 && qi < bank.length()) {
        let q: C_Question = bank[qi];
        let answered: boolean = state.c_picked >= 0;
        let options: string[] = [q.a, q.b, q.c, q.d];
        let cells: ui.View[] = [];
        let k: number = 0;
        while (k < 4) {
          let style: string = "default";
          if (answered) {
            if (k === q.correct) {
              style = "success";
            } else if (k === state.c_picked) {
              style = "danger";
            }
          }
          cells.push(ui.Cell(style, options[k], "c_answer", k, !answered));
          k = k + 1;
        }

        let feedback: ui.View[] = [];
        if (answered) {
          if (state.c_picked === q.correct) {
            feedback.push(ui.InsetBanner("success", "Correct!", "Nice one — that is right.", "", "", "check"));
          } else {
            feedback.push(ui.InsetBanner("danger", "Not quite", "The answer was " + options[q.correct] + ".", "", "", "close"));
          }
          let label: string = "Next question";
          if (pos + 1 >= total) {
            label = "See result";
          }
          feedback.push(ui.ActionBar("end", [
            ui.Button("primary", label, "c_next", 0, true)
          ]));
        }

          ui.SectionHeader("accent", "Question " + ui.numberToString(pos + 1) + " of " + ui.numberToString(total), q.category, ui.numberToString(state.c_correct) + " correct"),

          ui.Grid("default", 1, cells)
        ]));
        body.push(ui.Section("content", "", "", feedback));
      }
    }
  }

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:
    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
      sdk.call("Vera.Ask.text", ["prompt", "Two quick dinners using: " + names + ". One line each.", "maxWords", "60"], "onSuggested");
      return {c_ideas: "Thinking..."__PASSTHROUGH__};
    }
    function onSuggested(state: AppState, value: string): AppState { return {c_ideas: value__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  An answer starting with "error" is shown as a failure the person can try again. Call it only from a button's handler, never from view() or a ticker; and never for numbers the app works out itself or for anything known when the app is made.

Request: music trivia quiz

The section must do:
- A set of music trivia questions, each with a question text and four multiple-choice answers, one of which is correct, covering artists, albums, songs, and music history; the person reads each question, taps an answer, and the phone marks it right or wrong and moves to the next question until the round's question count is reached.
- round progress and final result screen
- the figure "Correct answers": how many questions the person has answered correctly so far this round (the plan works it out as entryCount; for entryCount = 7 that is 7)
- the figure "Score": points earned from correct answers this round (the plan works it out as correctAnswers * pointsPerCorrect; for correctAnswers = 7, pointsPerCorrect = 1 that is 7)

The person sets these on the screen and nothing else uses them yet; the section uses them:
- "Questions per round": state.questionCount

function c_shuffle(state: AppState, count: number): number[] {
  let bank: C_Question[] = c_bank();
  let total: number = bank.length();
  let pool: number[] = [];
  let i: number = 0;
  while (i < total) {
    pool.push(i);
    i = i + 1;
  }
  let seed: number = state.c_round * 7919 + count * 104729 + 17;
  let out: number[] = [];
  let n: number = 0;
  while (n < count && pool.length() > 0) {
    seed = math.randomStep(seed);
    let pick: number = math.randomBelow(seed, pool.length());
    let chosen: number = pool[pick];
    let kept: number[] = [];
    let j: number = 0;
    while (j < pool.length()) {
      if (j !== pick) {
        kept.push(pool[j]);
      }
      j = j + 1;
    }
    pool = kept;
    out.push(chosen);
    n = n + 1;
  }
  return out;
}

Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.

Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:
    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
      sdk.call("Vera.Ask.text", ["prompt", "Two quick dinners using: " + names + ". One line each.", "maxWords", "60"], "onSuggested");

Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion.     function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {

function c_start(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  let all: C_Question[] = c_buildQuestions();
  let picked: C_Question[] = [];
  let n: number = state.questionCount;
  if (n > all.length()) { n = all.length(); }
  if (n < 1) { n = 1; }
  let i: number = 0;
  while (i < n) {
    picked.push(all[i]);
    i = i + 1;
  }
  return {c_questions: picked, c_index: 0, c_score: 0, c_answered: false, c_picked: 0, c_finished: false, c_round: state.c_round + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

  if (state.c_answered || state.c_finished) {
    return {__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  let q: C_Question = state.c_questions[state.c_index];
  let gained: number = 0;
  if (value === q.correct) { gained = 1; }
  return {c_answered: true, c_picked: value, c_score: state.c_score + gained__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_next(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  if (!state.c_answered) {
    return {__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  let nextIndex: number = state.c_index + 1;
  if (nextIndex >= state.c_questions.length()) {
    return {c_finished: true, c_answered: false__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  return {c_index: nextIndex, c_answered: false, c_picked: 0__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

  return c_start(state, 0);
}

{
  let total: number = state.c_questions.length();

  }

    let q: C_Question = state.c_questions[state.c_index];

      }

      k = k + 1;
    }

      let verdict: string = "Not quite.";
      if (state.c_picked === q.correct) { verdict = "Correct!"; }
      rows.push(ui.InsetBanner("default", verdict, "The answer is " + q.choices[q.correct] + ".", "", "", ""));
      rows.push(ui.ActionBar("end", [ui.Button("primary", "Next question", "c_next", 0, true)]));
    }
  }
  if (state.c_finished) {
    rows.push(ui.InsetBanner("success", "Quiz complete", "You scored " + ui.numberToString(state.c_score) + " out of " + ui.numberToString(total) + ".", "", "", "star"));

      ui.NumberStat("default", "Questions", state.questionCount, "", "", 1, "in this quiz", "list")
    ]),
    ui.Column("default", rows)
  ]));
}

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:
    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
      sdk.call("Vera.Ask.text", ["prompt", "Two quick dinners using: " + names + ". One line each.", "maxWords", "60"], "onSuggested");
      return {c_ideas: "Thinking..."__PASSTHROUGH__};
    }

  An answer starting with "error" is shown as a failure the person can try again. Call it only from a button's handler, never from view() or a ticker; and never for numbers the app works out itself or for anything known when the app is made.

Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:

Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:
    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
      sdk.call("Vera.Ask.text", ["prompt", "Two quick dinners using: " + names + ". One line each.", "maxWords", "60"], "onSuggested");
      return {c_ideas: "Thinking..."__PASSTHROUGH__};
    }
    function onSuggested(state: AppState, value: string): AppState { return {c_ideas: value__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  An answer starting with "error" is shown as a failure the person can try again. Call it only from a button's handler, never from view() or a ticker; and never for numbers the app works out itself or for anything known when the app is made.

function c_weekNumber(state: AppState): number {
  let elapsed: number = (time.daysSinceEpoch() - state.c_firstWeekDay) * 86400;
  if (elapsed < 0) { elapsed = 0; }
  return math.floor((elapsed + 0) / 604800);
}

function c_turnIndex(state: AppState, weekNumber: number): number {
  if (state.siblingCount <= 0) { return 0; }
  return weekNumber % state.siblingCount;
}

function c_nameAt(state: AppState, index: number): string {
  let parts: string[] = strings.split(state.c_names, ",");
  let n: number = parts.length();
  if (n === 0) { return "Sibling " + ui.numberToString(index + 1); }
  let i: number = index % n;
  if (i < 0) { i = 0; }
  let name: string = strings.trim(parts[i]);
  if (name.length() === 0) { return "Sibling " + ui.numberToString(index + 1); }
  return name;
}

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:
    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
      sdk.call("Vera.Ask.text", ["prompt", "Two quick dinners using: " + names + ". One line each.", "maxWords", "60"], "onSuggested");
      return {c_ideas: "Thinking..."__PASSTHROUGH__};
    }
    function onSuggested(state: AppState, value: string): AppState { return {c_ideas: value__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  An answer starting with "error" is shown as a failure the person can try again. Call it only from a button's handler, never from view() or a ticker; and never for numbers the app works out itself or for anything known when the app is made.

Request: weekly cleaning turns for siblings

The section must do:
- The rotation advances one sibling each week, so turns are shared out evenly and repeat in order
- the figure "Week number": Which week of the rotation it is, counting from the first week the app was used (the plan works it out as floor((elapsed + 0) / 604800); for elapsed = 1209600 that is 2)
- the figure "Turn": Whose turn it is this week, as a position in the sibling list (the plan works it out as weekNumber % siblingCount; for weekNumber = 2, siblingCount = 2 that is 0)
- the figure "Turn number": The sibling whose turn it is this week, counting from 1 (the plan works it out as turnIndex + 1; for turnIndex = 0 that is 1)

The person sets these on the screen and nothing else uses them yet; the section uses them:
- "Week starts": state.weekStartIndex (the index of the chosen option: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday)
- "Siblings": state.siblingCount

The program already has these: use them, do not make your own:
- a checklist section, already on the screen, which has its list of items with how many are done, each ticked by a tap. Its state is in the program below. The section shows none of that again and works none of it out another way -- no second list, form, time, schedule or summary of the same things; what it needs of them it reads from that state.

Nothing they show is shown again: no second list, total, chart, Remove last or Start over button. While what the section works from is still empty, it shows one plain line saying what will appear and when, never a ui.EmptyState: the list above already has one (two empty states one under the other read as a broken screen).

@jsonable
class Item {
  label: string;
  detail: string;
  done: boolean;
}

class AppState {
  weekStartIndex: number;
  siblingCount: number;
  items7: Item[];
  settingsOpen: boolean;
}

function init(): AppState {
  let items7: Item[] = [
    {label: "Vacuuming", detail: "", done: false},
    {label: "Mopping floors", detail: "", done: false},
    {label: "Dusting", detail: "", done: false},
    {label: "Cleaning the bathroom", detail: "", done: false},
    {label: "Taking out the rubbish", detail: "", done: false},
    {label: "Tidying shared rooms", detail: "", done: false},
    {label: "Changing bed linen", detail: "", done: false},
    {label: "Wiping kitchen surfaces", detail: "", done: false}
  ];
  return {weekStartIndex: 0, siblingCount: 2, items7: items7, settingsOpen: false};
}

function share(a: number, b: number): number {
  if (b === 0) { return 0; }
  return a / b;
}



function set_weekStart(state: AppState, value: number): AppState {
  return {weekStartIndex: value, siblingCount: state.siblingCount, items7: state.items7, settingsOpen: state.settingsOpen};
}

function set_siblingCount(state: AppState, value: number): AppState {
  return {siblingCount: value, weekStartIndex: state.weekStartIndex, items7: state.items7, settingsOpen: state.settingsOpen};
}







function toggle7(state: AppState, index: number): AppState {
  let out: Item[] = [];
  let i: number = 0;
  while (i < state.items7.length()) {
    let it: Item = state.items7[i];
    if (i === index) {
      out.push({label: it.label, detail: it.detail, done: !it.done});
    } else {
      out.push(it);
    }
    i = i + 1;
  }
  return {items7: out, weekStartIndex: state.weekStartIndex, siblingCount: state.siblingCount, settingsOpen: state.settingsOpen};
}

function doneCount7(state: AppState): number {
  let n: number = 0;
  let i: number = 0;
  while (i < state.items7.length()) {
    let it: Item = state.items7[i];
    if (it.done) { n = n + 1; }
    i = i + 1;
  }
  return n;
}

function toggleSettings(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  return {settingsOpen: !state.settingsOpen, weekStartIndex: state.weekStartIndex, siblingCount: state.siblingCount, items7: state.items7};
}

function view(state: AppState): ui.View {
  let sections: ui.View[] = [];
  sections.push(ui.Header("default", "Chore Turns", "WEEKLY ROTA", "Split the weekly cleaning fairly between siblings", ""));
  {
      let weekStartValues: number[] = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 0];
      let weekStart: number = weekStartValues[state.weekStartIndex];
      let siblingCount: number = state.siblingCount;
      let weekDays: number = 7;
    sections.push(ui.Section("content", "", "", [ui.Select("default", "Week starts", ["Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"], state.weekStartIndex, "set_weekStart")]));
  }
  {
      let count: number = state.items7.length();
      let rows: ui.View[] = [];
      let j: number = 0;
      while (j < count) {
        let it: Item = state.items7[j];
        let icon: string = "";
        let subtitle: string = it.detail;
        if (it.done) { icon = "check"; subtitle = "done"; if (it.detail.length() > 0) { subtitle = it.detail + " - done"; } }
        rows.push(ui.ListItem("default", it.label, subtitle, "", "toggle7", j, true, icon));
        j = j + 1;
      }
      sections.push(ui.Section("content", "", "", [
        ui.When(count === 0, ui.EmptyState("default", "Nothing here", "Add an item to get started.", "", "", "pin")),
        ui.When(count > 0, ui.ListGroup("default", ui.numberToString(doneCount7(state)) + " of " + ui.numberToString(count) + " done - tap one to tick it", rows))
      ]));
    }
  {
    let settingsWord: string = "Show";
    if (state.settingsOpen) { settingsWord = "Hide"; }
    sections.push(ui.Section("supporting", "", "", [
      ui.ListItem("default", "Settings", "1 setting", settingsWord, "toggleSettings", 0, true, ""),
      ui.When(state.settingsOpen, ui.Column("default", [ui.NumberField("default", "Siblings", state.siblingCount, 2, 8, "set_siblingCount")]))
    ]));
  }
  return ui.AppTheme("clean", "", sections);
}

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. function c_rotationWeeks(state: AppState): number {
  let values: number[] = [1, 2, 3, 4];
  let idx: number = state.rotationLengthIndex;
  if (idx < 0) { idx = 0; }
  if (idx > 3) { idx = 3; }
  return values[idx];
}

function c_teamNames(state: AppState): string[] {
  let names: string[] = [];
  for (let e: LogEntry of state.entries) {
    let found: boolean = false;
    for (let n: string of names) {
      if (n === e.person) { found = true; }
    }
    if (!found) { names.push(e.person); }
  }
  return names;
}

function c_weeksElapsed(state: AppState): number {
  let start: number = strings.toNumber(state.startDate, 0);
  let elapsed: number = time.daysSinceEpoch() - start;
  if (elapsed < 0) { elapsed = 0; }
  let weeks: number = math.floor(elapsed / 7);
  let len: number = c_rotationWeeks(state);
  if (len <= 0) { return 0; }
  return math.floor(weeks / len);
}

function c_currentIndex(state: AppState): number {
  let size: number = c_teamNames(state).length();
  if (size === 0) { return 0; }
  return c_weeksElapsed(state) % size;
}

function c_nextIndex(state: AppState): number {
  let size: number = c_teamNames(state).length();
  if (size === 0) { return 0; }
  return (c_currentIndex(state) + 1) % size;
}

function c_nameAt(state: AppState, index: number): string {
  let names: string[] = c_teamNames(state);
  if (names.length() === 0) { return ""; }
  let i: number = index;
  if (i < 0) { i = 0; }
  if (i >= names.length()) { i = names.length() - 1; }
  return names[i];
}

function c_logCurrent(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  let names: string[] = c_teamNames(state);
  if (names.length() === 0) { return {__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  let person: string = c_nameAt(state, c_currentIndex(state));
  let out: LogEntry[] = [];
  for (let e: LogEntry of state.entries) { out.push(e); }
  let entry: LogEntry = {person: person, weekStart: time.daysSinceEpoch(), done: false, minute: time.hourOfDay() * 60 + time.minuteOfHour()};
  out.push(entry);
  return {entries: out__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_rotationWeeks(state: AppState): number {
  let values: number[] = [1, 2, 3, 4];
  let idx: number = state.rotationLengthIndex;
  if (idx < 0) { idx = 0; }
  if (idx > 3) { idx = 3; }
  return values[idx];
}

function c_teamNames(state: AppState): string[] {
  let names: string[] = [];
  for (let e: LogEntry of state.entries) {
    let found: boolean = false;
    for (let n: string of names) {
      if (n === e.person) { found = true; }
    }
    if (!found) { names.push(e.person); }
  }
  return names;
}

function c_weeksElapsed(state: AppState): number {
  let start: number = strings.toNumber(state.startDate, 0);
  let elapsed: number = time.daysSinceEpoch() - start;
  if (elapsed < 0) { elapsed = 0; }
  let weeks: number = math.floor(elapsed / 7);
  let len: number = c_rotationWeeks(state);
  if (len <= 0) { return 0; }
  return math.floor(weeks / len);
}

function c_currentIndex(state: AppState): number {
  let size: number = c_teamNames(state).length();
  if (size === 0) { return 0; }
  return c_weeksElapsed(state) % size;
}

function c_nextIndex(state: AppState): number {
  let size: number = c_teamNames(state).length();
  if (size === 0) { return 0; }
  return (c_currentIndex(state) + 1) % size;
}

function c_nameAt(state: AppState, index: number): string {
  let names: string[] = c_teamNames(state);
  if (names.length() === 0) { return ""; }
  let i: number = index;
  if (i < 0) { i = 0; }
  if (i >= names.length()) { i = names.length() - 1; }
  return names[i];
}

function c_logCurrent(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  let names: string[] = c_teamNames(state);
  if (names.length() === 0) { return {__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  let person: string = c_nameAt(state, c_currentIndex(state));
  let out: LogEntry[] = [];
  for (let e: LogEntry of state.entries) { out.push(e); }
  let entry: LogEntry = {person: person, weekStart: time.daysSinceEpoch(), done: false, minute: time.hourOfDay() * 60 + time.minuteOfHour()};
  out.push(entry);
  return {entries: out__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

the figure "Next person": Which team member is on kitchen duty next week (the plan works it out as (currentIndex + 1) % teamSize; for currentIndex = 2, teamSize = 6 that is 3)

    for (let s: string of seen) {

    i = i + 1;

}

Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.

- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.

  let n: number = state.items7.length();
  if (n === 0) { return 0; }
  let latest: number = state.items7[0].dueDay;
  let i: number = 1;
  while (i < n) {
    if (state.items7[i].dueDay > latest) { latest = state.items7[i].dueDay; }
    i = i + 1;
  }
  let d: number = state.today7 - latest;
  if (d < 0) { d = 0; }
  return d;
}

function c_daysSinceMillis(state: AppState): number {
  let n: number = state.items7.length();
  if (n === 0) { return 0; }
  let latest: number = state.items7[0].dueDay;
  let i: number = 1;
  while (i < n) {
    if (state.items7[i].dueDay > latest) { latest = state.items7[i].dueDay; }
    i = i + 1;
  }
  let nowSec: number = math.floor(time.nowMillis() / 1000);
  let changedSec: number = latest * 86400;
  let diff: number = nowSec - changedSec;
  if (diff < 0) { diff = 0; }
  return math.floor(diff / 86400);
}
