  return {c_renameIndex: -1, c_renameText: ""__PASSTHROUGH__};

    return {c_renameIndex: state.c_renameIndex, c_renameText: state.c_renameText__PASSTHROUGH__};
  }
  let out: DueItem[] = [];
  let i: number = 0;
  while (i < state.items7.length()) {
    let it: DueItem = state.items7[i];
    if (i === state.c_renameIndex) { out.push({name: name, dueDay: it.dueDay, lifeDays: it.lifeDays}); }
    else { out.push(it); }

- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.

- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.

- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.

  let count: number = state.entries.length();

  let latest: number = state.entries[0].minute;
  let i: number = 1;
  while (i < count) {
    if (state.entries[i].minute > latest) { latest = state.entries[i].minute; }
    i = i + 1;
  }
  let now: number = time.hourOfDay() * 60 + time.minuteOfHour();
  let elapsed: number = now - latest;
  if (elapsed < 0) { elapsed = elapsed + 1440; }
  return math.floor(elapsed);
}

  c_opts.push(ui.Cell("default", "Mixed", "c_pickType", 2, true));
  c_opts.push(ui.Cell("default", "Dry", "c_pickType", 3, true));

}

function c_parseDay(text: string): number {
  let t: string = strings.trim(text);

  let y: number = strings.toNumber(parts[0], -1);
  let m: number = strings.toNumber(parts[1], -1);
  let d: number = strings.toNumber(parts[2], -1);
  if (y < 1900 || y > 2200) { return -1; }
  if (m < 1 || m > 12) { return -1; }

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:

Request: badminton match score sheet

The section must do:
- the figure "Player A points": points won by Player A in the current game (the plan works it out as entryCount; for entryCount = 7 that is 7)
- the figure "Player B games": games won by Player B (the plan works it out as floor(entryCount / pointsPerGame); for entryCount = 21, pointsPerGame = 21 that is 1)
- the figure "Player B points": points won by Player B in the current game (the plan works it out as entryCount; for entryCount = 5 that is 5)
- the figure "Player A games": games won by Player A (the plan works it out as floor(entryCount / pointsPerGame); for entryCount = 42, pointsPerGame = 21 that is 2)
- the figure "Match won": whether a player has reached the games needed to win (a yes or a no worked out as 1 or 0: show it as Yes or No, or as words that say which, never as the number) (the plan works it out as max(gamesA, gamesB) >= gamesToWin; for gamesA = 2, gamesB = 1, gamesToWin = 2 that is 1)

The person sets these on the screen and nothing else uses them yet; the section uses them:
- "Games to win": state.gamesToWin
- "Points per game": state.pointsPerGame

The program already has these: use them, do not make your own:
- a list of entries: state.entries is LogEntry[] with the fields {player: string, game: number, minute: number}. Its form, its Add and Remove buttons and its rows are already on the screen. The section makes no list of its own for the same entries; to add one it copies state.entries into a new array, pushes a LogEntry (minute: time.hourOfDay() * 60 + time.minuteOfHour()) and returns {entries: thatArray __PASSTHROUGH__}.

Nothing they show is shown again: no second list, total, chart, Remove last or Start over button. While what the section works from is still empty, it shows one plain line saying what will appear and when, never a ui.EmptyState: the list above already has one (two empty states one under the other read as a broken screen).

Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.

- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.

Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:
    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
      sdk.call("Vera.Ask.text", ["prompt", "Two quick dinners using: " + names + ". One line each.", "maxWords", "60"], "onSuggested");

Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:
    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {

</fields>
<functions>
function c_entryCount(state: AppState): number {
  let n: number = 0;
  for (let d: Dose of state.doses7) {
    if (d.takenDay >= 0) { n = n + 1; }
  }
  return n;
}

function c_currentStreak(state: AppState): number {
  return c_entryCount(state);
}

function c_bestStreak(state: AppState, streakGoal: number): number {
  let entryCount: number = c_entryCount(state);
  if (streakGoal > entryCount) { return streakGoal; }
  return entryCount;
}

function c_setWeeklyGoal(state: AppState, value: number): AppState {
  let goal: number = math.round(value);
  if (goal < 1) { goal = 1; }
  if (goal > 7) { goal = 7; }
  return {c_weeklyGoal: goal__PASSTHROUGH__};
}
</functions>
<view>
{
  let c_count: number = state.doses7.length();
  let c_streakGoal: number = state.c_weeklyGoal;
  let c_current: number = c_currentStreak(state);
  let c_best: number = c_bestStreak(state, c_streakGoal);
  let c_goal: number = c_streakGoal;
  if (c_best > c_goal) { c_goal = c_best; }
  let c_currentText: string = ui.numberToString(c_current) + " days";
  if (c_current === 1) { c_currentText = "1 day"; }
  let c_bestText: string = ui.numberToString(c_best) + " days";
  if (c_best === 1) { c_bestText = "1 day"; }
  let c_body: ui.View[] = [];
  c_body.push(ui.NumberField("default", "Weekly goal (days)", state.c_weeklyGoal, 1, 7, "c_setWeeklyGoal"));
  if (c_count === 0) {
    c_body.push(ui.Text("muted", "Your current and best streak appear here once you add a workout above."));
  } else {
    c_body.push(ui.MetricGroup("default", 2, [
      ui.NumberStat("accent", "Current streak", c_current, "", " days", 1, "consecutive days up to today", "star"),
      ui.NumberStat("default", "Best streak", c_best, "", " days", 1, "longest run ever logged", "chart")
    ]));
    c_body.push(ui.Progress("accent", "Best streak toward " + ui.numberToString(c_goal) + " days", c_best, c_goal));
  }
  sections.push(ui.Section("summary", "Streaks", "", c_body));
}
</view>

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:
    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
      sdk.call("Vera.Ask.text", ["prompt", "Two quick dinners using: " + names + ". One line each.", "maxWords", "60"], "onSuggested");
      return {c_ideas: "Thinking..."__PASSTHROUGH__};
    }
    function onSuggested(state: AppState, value: string): AppState { return {c_ideas: value__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  An answer starting with "error" is shown as a failure the person can try again. Call it only from a button's handler, never from view() or a ticker; and never for numbers the app works out itself or for anything known when the app is made.

function c_longestStreak(state: AppState): number {
  let entryCount: number = state.entries.length();
  let current: number = c_currentStreak(state);
  if (entryCount > current) { return entryCount; }
  return current;
}

function c_currentStreak(state: AppState): number {
  let today: number = time.daysSinceEpoch();
  let run: number = 0;
  let day: number = today;
  let going: boolean = true;
  while (going) {
    let has: boolean = false;
    for (let e: LogEntry of state.entries) {
      if (e.entryDate === day) { has = true; }
    }
    if (has) {
      run = run + 1;
      day = day - 1;
    } else {
      if (run === 0 && day === today) {
        day = day - 1;
      } else {
        going = false;
      }
    }
  }
  return run;
}

      out.push({entryDate: e.entryDate, noteItem: strings.trim(state.c_editNote), minute: e.minute});

function c_longestStreak(state: AppState): number {
  let best: number = 0;
  let run: number = 0;
  let prev: number = -999999;
  let i: number = 0;
  while (i < state.entries.length()) {
    let d: number = state.entries[i].entryDate;
    if (d !== prev) {
      if (prev !== -999999 && d === prev + 1) {
        run = run + 1;
      } else {
        run = 1;
      }
      if (run > best) { best = run; }
      prev = d;
    }
    i = i + 1;
  }
  return best;
}

function c_currentStreak(state: AppState): number {
  let today: number = time.daysSinceEpoch();
  let run: number = 0;
  let day: number = today;
  let going: boolean = true;
  while (going) {
    let has: boolean = false;
    for (let e: LogEntry of state.entries) {
      if (e.entryDate === day) { has = true; }
    }
    if (has) {
      run = run + 1;
      day = day - 1;
    } else {
      if (run === 0 && day === today) {
        day = day - 1;
      } else {
        going = false;
      }
    }
  }
  return run;
}

function c_keptStreak(state: AppState, index: number): boolean {
  if (index < 0 || index >= state.entries.length()) { return false; }
  let d: number = state.entries[index].entryDate;
  let i: number = 0;
  while (i < state.entries.length()) {
    if (i !== index && state.entries[i].entryDate === d - 1) { return true; }
    i = i + 1;
  }
  return false;
}

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:
    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
      sdk.call("Vera.Ask.text", ["prompt", "Two quick dinners using: " + names + ". One line each.", "maxWords", "60"], "onSuggested");
      return {c_ideas: "Thinking..."__PASSTHROUGH__};
    }
    function onSuggested(state: AppState, value: string): AppState { return {c_ideas: value__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  An answer starting with "error" is shown as a failure the person can try again. Call it only from a button's handler, never from view() or a ticker; and never for numbers the app works out itself or for anything known when the app is made.

</fields>

function c_streak(state: AppState): number {
  let count: number = 0;
  let i: number = state.entries.length() - 1;
  let going: boolean = true;
  while (i >= 0 && going) {
    if (state.entries[i].wakeTime <= state.targetTime) {
      count = count + 1;
      i = i - 1;
    } else {
      going = false;
    }
  }
  return count;
}
</functions>
<view>
{
  let c_total: number = state.entries.length();
  let c_current: number = c_streak(state);
  let c_best: number = 0;
  let c_run: number = 0;
  let c_j: number = 0;
  while (c_j < c_total) {
    if (state.entries[c_j].wakeTime <= state.targetTime) {
      c_run = c_run + 1;
      if (c_run > c_best) { c_best = c_run; }
    } else {
      c_run = 0;
    }
    c_j = c_j + 1;
  }
  let c_children: ui.View[] = [];
  if (c_total === 0) {
    c_children.push(ui.Text("body", "Your current streak appears here once you log a wake-up."));
  } else {
    c_children.push(ui.MetricGroup("default", 2, [
      ui.NumberStat("accent", "Current streak", c_current, "", "", 1, "wake-ups by " + ui.clockToString(state.targetTime), "star"),
      ui.NumberStat("default", "Best streak", c_best, "", "", 1, "of " + ui.numberToString(c_total) + " logged", "chart")
    ]));
    let c_dates: ui.View[] = [];
    let c_k: number = c_total - 1;
    while (c_k >= 0 && c_k > c_total - 8) {
      let c_e: LogEntry = state.entries[c_k];
      let c_day: number = time.daysSinceEpoch() - (c_total - 1 - c_k);
      let c_ok: string = "late";
      if (c_e.wakeTime <= state.targetTime) { c_ok = "early"; }
      c_dates.push(ui.ListItem("default", ui.dateToString(c_day), c_ok, ui.clockToString(c_e.wakeTime), "", 0, true, "calendar"));
      c_k = c_k - 1;
    }
    c_children.push(ui.SectionHeader("default", "Logged dates", "Most recent first", ui.numberToString(c_total)));
    c_children.push(ui.ListGroup("default", "", c_dates));
  }
  sections.push(ui.Section("summary", "", "", c_children));
}
</view>

<classes>

<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>

</functions>

- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.

- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.

- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.

<functions>
function c_hasLower(p: string): number {
  if (p !== strings.toUpperCase(p)) { return 1; }
  return 0;
}

function c_hasUpper(p: string): number {
  if (p !== strings.toLowerCase(p)) { return 1; }
  return 0;
}

function c_hasDigit(p: string): number {
  for (let ch: string of p) {
    if (ch >= "0" && ch <= "9") { return 1; }
  }
  return 0;
}

function c_hasSymbol(p: string): number {
  for (let ch: string of p) {
    let isLower: boolean = ch >= "a" && ch <= "z";
    let isUpper: boolean = ch >= "A" && ch <= "Z";
    let isDigit: boolean = ch >= "0" && ch <= "9";
    if (!isLower && !isUpper && !isDigit) { return 1; }
  }
  return 0;
}

function c_lengthScore(len: number): number {
  return math.min(40, len * 4);
}

function c_lengthBonus(len: number, minLength: number): number {
  if (len >= minLength) { return 20; }
  return 0;
}

function c_varietyScore(variety: number): number {
  return variety * 10;
}

function c_strengthScore(len: number, variety: number, minLength: number, maxScore: number): number {
  return math.min(maxScore, c_lengthScore(len) + c_varietyScore(variety) + c_lengthBonus(len, minLength));
}

function c_yesNo(flag: number): string {
  if (flag === 1) { return "Yes"; }
  return "No";
}

function c_masked(p: string): string {
  let out: string = "";
  let i: number = 0;
  let n: number = strings.length(p);
  while (i < n) {
    out = out + "\u2022";
    i = i + 1;
  }
  return out;
}

function c_toggleReveal(state: AppState, value: boolean): AppState {
  return {c_reveal: value__PASSTHROUGH__};
}
</functions>

    ui.KeyValueGroup("default", 2, [
      ui.KeyValueItem("default", "Length score", ui.numberToString(c_lenScore), "up to 40"),
      ui.KeyValueItem("default", "Length bonus", ui.numberToString(c_lenBonus), "at " + ui.numberToString(c_minLength) + " characters"),

<functions>
function c_hasLower(p: string): number {
  if (p !== strings.toUpperCase(p)) { return 1; }
  return 0;
}

function c_hasUpper(p: string): number {
  if (p !== strings.toLowerCase(p)) { return 1; }
  return 0;
}

function c_hasDigit(p: string): number {
  for (let ch: string of p) {
    if (ch >= "0" && ch <= "9") { return 1; }
  }
  return 0;
}

function c_hasSymbol(p: string): number {
  for (let ch: string of p) {
    let isLower: boolean = ch >= "a" && ch <= "z";
    let isUpper: boolean = ch >= "A" && ch <= "Z";
    let isDigit: boolean = ch >= "0" && ch <= "9";
    if (!isLower && !isUpper && !isDigit) { return 1; }
  }
  return 0;
}

function c_lengthScore(len: number): number {
  return math.min(40, len * 4);
}

function c_lengthBonus(len: number, minLength: number): number {
  if (len >= minLength) { return 20; }
  return 0;
}

function c_varietyScore(variety: number): number {
  return variety * 10;
}

function c_strengthScore(len: number, variety: number, minLength: number, maxScore: number): number {
  return math.min(maxScore, c_lengthScore(len) + c_varietyScore(variety) + c_lengthBonus(len, minLength));
}

function c_yesNo(flag: number): string {
  if (flag === 1) { return "Yes"; }
  return "No";
}
</functions>

{
  let c_pw: string = state.password;
  let c_len: number = strings.length(c_pw);
  let c_minLength: number = 12;
  let c_maxScore: number = 100;

  let c_upper: number = c_hasUpper(c_pw);
  let c_digit: number = c_hasDigit(c_pw);
  let c_symbol: number = c_hasSymbol(c_pw);
  let c_variety: number = c_lower + c_upper + c_digit + c_symbol;
  let c_lenScore: number = c_lengthScore(c_len);
  let c_lenBonus: number = c_lengthBonus(c_len, c_minLength);
  let c_varScore: number = c_varietyScore(c_variety);
  let c_score: number = c_strengthScore(c_len, c_variety, c_minLength, c_maxScore);
  let c_frac: number = share(c_score, c_maxScore);
  let c_tone: string = "danger";
  if (c_score >= 80) {
    c_tone = "success";
  } else if (c_score >= 50) {

  }

    ]),

  ]));
  sections.push(ui.Section("content", "Character kinds", "What your password mixes", [

      ui.Stat("default", "Lowercase", c_yesNo(c_lower), "", ""),

    ])
  ]));

    ui.KeyValueGroup("default", 2, [
      ui.KeyValueItem("default", "Length score", ui.numberToString(c_lenScore), "up to 40"),

      ui.KeyValueItem("default", "Variety", ui.numberToString(c_variety), "kinds used"),
      ui.KeyValueItem("default", "Variety score", ui.numberToString(c_varScore), "up to 40"),

    ])
  ]));

  }
  if (c_upper === 0) {
    c_hints.push(ui.ListItem("default", "Add an uppercase letter", "Adds a character kind", "", "", 0, true, "plus"));
  }
  if (c_digit === 0) {
    c_hints.push(ui.ListItem("default", "Add a number", "Adds a character kind", "", "", 0, true, "plus"));
  }
  if (c_symbol === 0) {
    c_hints.push(ui.ListItem("default", "Add a symbol", "Adds a character kind", "", "", 0, true, "plus"));
  }
  if (c_score >= c_maxScore) {
    c_hints.push(ui.ListItem("success", "Nothing missing", "This password reaches the top score", "", "", 0, true, "check"));
  }

    ui.ListGroup("default", "", c_hints)

Request: check password strength

The section must do:
- the figure "Length": how many characters the password has (the plan works it out as len(password); for its example that is 11)
- the figure "Lowercase": whether the password has a lowercase letter (a yes or a no worked out as 1 or 0: show it as Yes or No, or as words that say which, never as the number) (the plan works it out as password != password.toUpperCase(); for its example that is 1)
- the figure "Uppercase": whether the password has an uppercase letter (a yes or a no worked out as 1 or 0: show it as Yes or No, or as words that say which, never as the number) (the plan works it out as password != password.toLowerCase(); for its example that is 1)
- the figure "Number": whether the password has a digit (a yes or a no worked out as 1 or 0: show it as Yes or No, or as words that say which, never as the number) (the plan works it out as password != password.replace(/[0-9]/g, ''); for its example that is 1)
- the figure "Symbol": whether the password has a symbol (a yes or a no worked out as 1 or 0: show it as Yes or No, or as words that say which, never as the number) (the plan works it out as password != password.replace(/[^A-Za-z0-9]/g, ''); for its example that is 1)
- the figure "Length score": points for length, up to 40 (the plan works it out as min(40, length * 4); for length = 11 that is 40)
- the figure "Length bonus": extra points for reaching a good length (the plan works it out as length >= minLength ? 20 : 0; for length = 11, minLength = 12 that is 0)
- the figure "Strength score": overall strength from 0 to 100 (the plan works it out as min(maxScore, lengthScore + varietyScore + lengthBonus); for lengthScore = 40, varietyScore = 40, lengthBonus = 0, maxScore = 100 that is 80)
- the figure "Variety": how many kinds of characters are used (the plan works it out as hasLower + hasUpper + hasDigit + hasSymbol; for hasLower = 1, hasUpper = 1, hasDigit = 1, hasSymbol = 1 that is 4)
- the figure "Variety score": points for mixing character kinds, up to 40 (the plan works it out as variety * 10; for variety = 4 that is 40)
- the figure "Strength": the score as a fraction for the strength bar (the plan works it out as score / maxScore; for score = 80, maxScore = 100 that is 0.8)

<fields>

Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.

- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.

    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {

function c_keyOf(line: string, ignoreCase: boolean, trimSpaces: boolean): string {
  let k: string = line;
  if (trimSpaces) { k = strings.trim(k); }
  if (ignoreCase) { k = strings.toLowerCase(k); }
  return k;
}

function c_splitLines(text: string): string[] {
  let out: string[] = [];
  if (strings.length(text) === 0) { return out; }
  let parts: string[] = strings.split(text, "\n");
  for (let p: string of parts) {
    let q: string = p;
    if (strings.endsWith(q, "\r")) {
      q = strings.substring(q, 0, strings.length(q) - 1);
    }
    out.push(q);
  }
  return out;
}

function c_lineCount(text: string): number {
  return c_splitLines(text).length();
}

function c_uniqueLines(text: string, ignoreCase: boolean, trimSpaces: boolean): string[] {
  let lines: string[] = c_splitLines(text);
  let seen: string[] = [];
  let out: string[] = [];
  for (let line: string of lines) {
    let k: string = c_keyOf(line, ignoreCase, trimSpaces);
    let found: boolean = false;
    for (let s: string of seen) {
      if (s === k) { found = true; }
    }
    if (!found) {
      seen.push(k);
      out.push(line);
    }
  }
  return out;
}

function c_joinLines(lines: string[]): string {
  let out: string = "";
  let i: number = 0;
  while (i < lines.length()) {
    if (i > 0) { out = out + "\n"; }
    out = out + lines[i];
    i = i + 1;
  }
  return out;
}

function c_copy(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  let unique: string[] = c_uniqueLines(state.inputText, state.ignoreCase, state.trimSpaces);
  let cleaned: string = c_joinLines(unique);
  if (strings.length(cleaned) === 0) {
    return {c_copyStatus: "Nothing to copy yet."__PASSTHROUGH__};

function c_keyOf(line: string, ignoreCase: boolean, trimSpaces: boolean): string {
  let k: string = line;
  if (trimSpaces) { k = strings.trim(k); }
  if (ignoreCase) { k = strings.toLowerCase(k); }
  return k;

function c_splitLines(text: string): string[] {
  let out: string[] = [];
  if (strings.length(text) === 0) { return out; }
  let parts: string[] = strings.split(text, "\n");
  for (let p: string of parts) {
    let q: string = p;
    if (strings.endsWith(q, "\r")) {
      q = strings.substring(q, 0, strings.length(q) - 1);
    }
    out.push(q);
  }
  return out;
}

function c_lineCount(text: string): number {
  return c_splitLines(text).length();
}

function c_uniqueLines(text: string, ignoreCase: boolean, trimSpaces: boolean): string[] {
  let lines: string[] = c_splitLines(text);
  let seen: string[] = [];
  let out: string[] = [];
  for (let line: string of lines) {
    let k: string = c_keyOf(line, ignoreCase, trimSpaces);
    let found: boolean = false;
    for (let s: string of seen) {
      if (s === k) { found = true; }
    }
    if (!found) {
      seen.push(k);
      out.push(line);
    }
  }
  return out;
}

function c_joinLines(lines: string[]): string {
  let out: string = "";
  let i: number = 0;
  while (i < lines.length()) {
    if (i > 0) { out = out + "\n"; }
    out = out + lines[i];
    i = i + 1;
  }
  return out;
}

messages.content:
Now you do not write a whole program. You add ONE section to a VERA-L program that already exists, and you write only that section, in exactly this form and nothing else:
<classes>
any @jsonable record classes the section needs, or nothing
</classes>
<fields>
one state field per line, as  name: type = initial value  (or nothing)
</fields>
<functions>
the handlers and helper functions the section needs
</functions>
<view>
statements that build the section and add it with sections.push(ui.Section(...));
</view>
Rules for the section:
- Begin the name of every class, field and function with c_ (classes with C_), so nothing clashes with the program.
- A handler returns only the fields it changes, followed by __PASSTHROUGH__ just before the closing brace, which stands for every other field of the state kept as it is: return {c_count: state.c_count + 1__PASSTHROUGH__};
- The view statements run inside view(state): they may read any state field, but the local variables of the program's other sections are not visible there.
- Do not repeat, change or restyle anything the program already has. Do what the section must do, completely.
- If the program already has a clock (Start, Stop, Reset buttons, a time shown) or a list of entries with its own Add button, the section draws no clock, no Start/Stop/Reset buttons and no second list of the same entries: it works with that state and shows only what is new.
- A message about an empty or wrong field (such as "Enter a task name") is shown only after the person has tried to add it, never while the field is still untouched.
- Show each piece of information once: no heading and caption that say the same thing, and no second view (a table, "splits") of entries the program already lists in rows. A figure is a progress bar or a number, not both; a list the program already has (its stops, its entries) is not listed again with a button added to each row -- the button goes where the program can take it, or the section names the item to act on; and one set of tabs or switches for one choice.
- A list the section keeps that starts empty has its own way to add to it, and to remove from it: an empty list nothing can fill is a dead end (Chore stars: "No rewards yet" with no way to add one).
- Every number the section shows is worked out from something on the screen or named in the request: progress toward a goal needs the goal, set on the screen or fixed by the request, not a percent of nothing.
- Never write a phone number, address or other real-world contact the request did not give: a made-up number (such as +1 800 555 0100) looks real to the person. Show a field for the person to fill in, or say to call their local emergency number.
- When some of the needs cannot be done but others can, write the section for the ones that can and add, for each one that cannot, <cannot need="the need, copied exactly">one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> beside it. Answer a bare <cannot> only when none can be done.
- A need declined has no button or row that claims to do it. If the section offers the nearest thing instead (an event in the phone calendar for a notification it cannot send), its button says that thing ("Add to calendar"), and the <cannot> sentence says what is offered instead. A notice saying it cannot beside a button named for the same thing reads as broken.
- A need the section does in its own way is done, not declined: guidance written out as rows is the care card or tips card asked for, a list is a "card", a field the person fills in is a setting. <cannot need> is only for what the person does not get at all on this screen, never for how it looks.
- What the phone or another app must do, the section does with sdk.call from a handler, calling ONLY targets from "Phone functions found" in the request (and "Vera.Ask.text", as said below), copied exactly, with the parameters they show, values from the screen's state. Its answer handler shows what came back: an answer starting with "declined" or "error" is a failure, anything else succeeded.
- A function that opens another app with the action ready for the person to confirm (a message filled in, a contact form, a route) does the job: use it, and say on the screen that the person confirms it there.
- Before answering <cannot>, go through the phone functions found for each need: when one does it -- even by parts, such as audio samples written to a renderer, or the flashlight switched on and off -- write the section with it.
- A need worded as something to do inside this app that the app cannot do (it has no such component) is not refused if a function found does the nearest useful thing for the person -- shows or opens the same thing in the app made for it: write the section with that function, and say in a line on the screen what it does instead.
- Words written from what the person entered (suggestions, recipes, ideas) are never declined: "Vera.Ask.text" writes them, as said below.
- If none of the phone functions found does what is needed, or it needs something the phone cannot give a program (a camera, a live feed, the person's location), decline that need as above, beside the rest; a bare <cannot>one short sentence for the person using the app, in plain words about their phone and its apps: what this app cannot do, and why. Never mention the language, the section, sdk.call or code</cannot> only when none of the needs can be done. Never fake it, never pretend a call happened, never call a target that is not listed.
- Suggestions, ideas, recipes, tips or questions made FROM WHAT THE PERSON ENTERED (dinners from the items in their pantry, questions from their notes, a plan from the times they set) are written by the model while the app runs, never by the section: a fixed sentence with their words pasted in ("Roast vegetable tray, uses Spinach") is not a suggestion. The section has a button that asks, a "pending" text while it waits, and the answer shown as text:
    function suggest(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
      sdk.call("Vera.Ask.text", ["prompt", "Two quick dinners using: " + names + ". One line each.", "maxWords", "60"], "onSuggested");
      return {c_ideas: "Thinking..."__PASSTHROUGH__};
    }
    function onSuggested(state: AppState, value: string): AppState { return {c_ideas: value__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  An answer starting with "error" is shown as a failure the person can try again. Call it only from a button's handler, never from view() or a ticker; and never for numbers the app works out itself or for anything known when the app is made.

<classes>

</classes>
<fields>
c_words: string[] = ["apple", "brisk", "candid", "dwell", "eager", "fable", "grasp", "humble", "ivory", "jolly", "kneel", "lucid", "mellow", "nimble", "orbit", "placid", "quaint", "rustic", "subtle", "tender"]
c_index: number = 0
c_typed: string = ""
c_correct: number = 0
c_attempts: number = 0
c_wrong: boolean = false
c_done: boolean = false
</fields>
<functions>
function c_currentWord(state: AppState): string {
  if (state.c_index >= state.c_words.length()) { return ""; }
  return state.c_words[state.c_index];
}

function c_advance(state: AppState, attempts: number, correct: number): AppState {
  let nextIndex: number = state.c_index + 1;
  let done: boolean = nextIndex >= state.c_words.length() || nextIndex >= state.wordCount;
  return {c_index: nextIndex, c_typed: "", c_correct: correct, c_attempts: attempts, c_wrong: false, c_done: done__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_onType(state: AppState, value: string): AppState {
  if (state.c_done) { return {c_typed: value__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  let target: string = c_currentWord(state);
  if (target === "") { return {c_typed: value__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  let guess: string = strings.trim(strings.toLowerCase(value));
  if (guess === strings.toLowerCase(target)) {
    return c_advance(state, state.c_attempts + 1, state.c_correct + 1);
  }
  return {c_typed: value, c_wrong: false__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_onCheck(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  if (state.c_done) { return {__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  let target: string = c_currentWord(state);
  if (target === "") { return {__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  let guess: string = strings.trim(strings.toLowerCase(state.c_typed));
  if (guess === "") { return {c_wrong: true__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  let attempts: number = state.c_attempts + 1;
  if (guess === strings.toLowerCase(target)) {
    return c_advance(state, attempts, state.c_correct + 1);
  }
  return {c_attempts: attempts, c_wrong: true__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_onSkip(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  if (state.c_done) { return {__PASSTHROUGH__}; }
  return c_advance(state, state.c_attempts + 1, state.c_correct);
}

function c_onRestart(state: AppState, ignored: number): AppState {
  return {c_index: 0, c_typed: "", c_correct: 0, c_attempts: 0, c_wrong: false, c_done: false__PASSTHROUGH__};
}

function c_wpm(state: AppState): number {
  let seconds: number = state.elapsedMs / 1000;
  if (seconds <= 0) { return 0; }
  return state.c_correct / (seconds / 60);
}

function c_accuracy(state: AppState): number {
  let denom: number = math.max(state.c_attempts, 1);
  return state.c_correct / denom * 100;
}
</functions>
<view>
let c_target: string = c_currentWord(state);
let c_typedCount: number = state.c_correct;
let c_wpmValue: number = c_wpm(state);
let c_accValue: number = c_accuracy(state);
let c_goal: number = state.wordCount;
let c_children: ui.View[] = [];
if (state.c_done) {
  c_children.push(ui.InsetBanner("success", "Drill complete", "You typed " + ui.numberToString(c_typedCount) + " words correctly.", "", "", "check"));
} else {
  c_children.push(ui.Text("eyebrow", "Word " + ui.numberToString(state.c_index + 1) + " of " + ui.numberToString(c_goal)));
  c_children.push(ui.Text("display", c_target));
  c_children.push(ui.TextField("default", "Type the word", state.c_typed, "c_onType"));
  c_children.push(ui.Text("caption", "It checks itself the moment the word matches."));
  c_children.push(ui.When(state.c_wrong, ui.Text("danger", "Not quite — check the spelling and try again.")));
  c_children.push(ui.ActionBar("end", [
    ui.Button("primary", "Check", "c_onCheck", 0, true),
    ui.Button("secondary", "Skip", "c_onSkip", 0, true)
  ]));
}
c_children.push(ui.MetricGroup("default", 3, [
  ui.NumberStat("default", "Words typed", c_typedCount, "", "", 1, "of " + ui.numberToString(c_goal), "check"),
  ui.NumberStat("accent", "Words per minute", c_wpmValue, "", "", 1, "", "chart"),
  ui.NumberStat("default", "Accuracy", c_accValue, "", "%", 1, "", "star")
]));
c_children.push(ui.Progress("accent", "Words typed", c_typedCount, c_goal));
if (state.c_done) {
  c_children.push(ui.ActionBar("end", [ui.Button("secondary", "Type again", "c_onRestart", 0, true)]));
}
sections.push(ui.Section("content", "Typing drill", "Type each word exactly — it checks itself", c_children));
</view>
